etymology: Webster (1828) enters MAT’INS without an etymology note; this entry does not supply one.
biblical_def: Webster (1828) defines matins as “Morning worship or service; morning prayers or songs,” and, as a set time, “the first canonical hour in the Romish church.” The morning hour of prayer is biblical before it is canonical: “My voice shalt thou hear in the morning, O LORD; in the morning will I direct my prayer unto thee, and will look up” (Psa 5:3). Jesus, “rising up a great while before day, he went out, and departed into a solitary place, and there prayed” (Mar 1:35). God’s mercies “are new every morning” (Lam 3:23).

pos: n. (an inscription in memory of the dead)
biblical_def: Webster (1828) defines an epitaph as “An inscription on a monument, in honor or memory of the dead.” His illustrations are sharp: “The epitaphs of the present day are crammed with fulsome compliments never merited,” and a warning against “a towering monument--it may be a lying epitaph.” Scripture’s epitaphs are short and true. Of Enoch: “he had this testimony, that he pleased God” (Heb 11:5). Of David: “after he had served his own generation by the will of God, fell on sleep” (Act 13:36). Of the kings of Israel and Judah, the record was plain whether each “did that which was right in the sight of the LORD” or not (2Ki 18:3).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): EPITAPH, an inscription on a monument in honor or memory of the dead; a eulogy not meant to be engraved.
webster_full: EP'ITAPH, noun [Gr. a sepulcher.]
1. An inscription on a monument, in honor or memory of the dead.
The epitaphs of the present day are crammed with fulsome compliments never merited.
Can you look forward to the honor of a decorated coffin, a splendid funeral, a towering monument--it may be a lying epitaph
2. An eulogy, in prose or verse, composed without any intent to be engraven on a monument, as that on Alexander:
'Sufficit huic tumulus, cui non sufficeret orbis.'

And he did that which was right in the sight of the LORD, according to all that David his father did.
corruption_summary: Epitaphs are now mostly sentiment; Webster already complained of “fulsome compliments never merited.”
corruption_paragraphs: Webster’s own examples attack flattering epitaphs and even “a lying epitaph.” The danger has only grown with the custom of praising every life.
Scripture’s verdicts on the dead are brief and honest (2Ki 18:3; Heb 11:5). The epitaph that matters is God’s.

etymology: Webster (1828) enters SEP’ULTURE without an etymology note; this entry does not supply one.
biblical_def: Webster (1828) defines sepulture as “Burial” and “the act of depositing the dead body of a human being in the grave.” Scripture treats burial as an act of honour and faith. Abraham bought a field to bury Sarah (Gen 23:19). Joseph made his brethren swear to carry up his bones (Gen 50:25). Jesus received burial from Joseph of Arimathaea, who “laid it in his own new tomb” (Mat 27:60). The body is sown in hope: “It is sown in corruption; it is raised in incorruption” (1Co 15:42).

biblical_def: Webster (1828) defines a cenotaph as “An empty tomb erected in honor of some deceased person; a monument erected to one who is buried elsewhere.” Scripture has its memorials of the absent. Absalom, with no son, “reared up for himself a pillar” to keep his name (2Sa 18:18). Moses has no tomb at all: “no man knoweth of his sepulchre unto this day” (Deu 34:6). And one tomb is empty for a different reason: “He is not here: for he is risen, as he said. Come, see the place where the Lord lay” (Mat 28:6).

biblical_def: Webster (1828) defines a litany as “A solemn form of supplication, used in public worship.” He adds that “Supplications for the appeasing of God’s wrath, were by the Greek church termed litanies, by the Latin, rogations.” Scripture’s public supplications include Solomon’s prayer at the temple (1Ki 8:45), Daniel’s confession, “O Lord, hear; O Lord, forgive; O Lord, hearken and do” (Dan 9:19), and Paul’s charge “that, first of all, supplications, prayers, intercessions, and giving of thanks, be made for all men” (1Ti 2:1). The warning is against prayer by repetition alone: “use not vain repetitions, as the heathen do” (Mat 6:7).

pos: n. (an abridgment; the book of the daily office)
etymology: Webster (1828): [Latin breviarium, from brevis, short. See Brief.]
biblical_def: Webster (1828) gives two senses of breviary: “An abridgment; a compend; an epitome,” and “A book containing the daily service of the Romish church,” composed of matins, lauds, the hours and compline. The first sense is the root: something short. The Psalter was Israel’s prayer book, and the psalmist kept fixed times: “Seven times a day do I praise thee because of thy righteous judgments” (Psa 119:164); “Evening, and morning, and at noon, will I pray” (Psa 55:17). Daniel prayed three times a day (Dan 6:10). No book of hours replaces the word itself (2Ti 3:16).

Brief.]

etymology: Webster (1828): [Gr. against, and a hymn, from to sing. See Hymn.]
biblical_def: Webster (1828) defines an anthem as “A hymn sung in alternate parts,” and in his own day “a sacred tune or piece of music set to words, taken from the psalms or other parts of the scriptures.” Singing in answering parts is old: Israel’s women “answered one another as they played” (1Sa 18:7), and the Levites sang “together by course in praising and giving thanks unto the LORD; because he is good, for his mercy endureth for ever” (Ezr 3:11). Of the seraphim, “one cried unto another, and said, Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of hosts” (Isa 6:3). Believers are to speak “in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs” (Eph 5:19).

biblical_def: Webster (1828) defines a requiem as, “In the Romish church, a hymn or mass sung for the dead, for the rest of his soul; so called from the first word.” A second sense, “Rest; quiet; peace,” he marks as not in use. The practice assumes that the living can help the dead. Scripture says: “it is appointed unto men once to die, but after this the judgment” (Heb 9:27). Rest for the dead is promised to those who die in the Lord: “Blessed are the dead which die in the Lord from henceforth ... that they may rest from their labours” (Rev 14:13). Paul, being absent from the body, expected to be “present with the Lord” (2Co 5:8).

pos: n. (shaving the head; entrance into holy orders)
etymology: Webster (1828): [Latin tonsura, from tonsus, shaved; tondeo, to clip or shave.]
biblical_def: Webster (1828) defines tonsure as “The act of clipping the hair, or of shaving the head; or the state of being shorn.” In the Romish church it is “the first ceremony used for devoting a person to the service of God and the church,” given by a bishop who “cuts off a part of his hair with prayers and benedictions,” so that “tonsure is used to denote entrance or admission into holy orders.” Scripture’s nearest rite is the Nazarite’s, who let his hair grow and then shaved it “at the door of the tabernacle of the congregation” when his vow ended (Num 6:18). Paul once shaved his head, “for he had a vow” (Act 18:18). The priests of Israel were told, “They shall not make baldness upon their head” (Lev 21:5).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): TONSURE, clipping the hair or shaving the head; in the Romish church, the first ceremony devoting a person to the church, the entrance into holy orders; the priest’s crown.
webster_full: TON'SURE, noun [Latin tonsura, from tonsus, shaved; tondeo, to clip or shave.]
1. The act of clipping the hair, or of shaving the head; or the state of being shorn.

2. In the Romish church, tonsure is the first ceremony used for devoting a person to the service of God and the church; the first degree of the clericate, given by a bishop, who cuts off a part of his hair with prayers and benedictions. Hence tonsure is used to denote entrance or admission into holy orders.
3. In the Romish church, the corona or crown which priests wear as a mark of their order and of their rank in the church.

etymology: Webster (1828) enters CHANTRY without an etymology note; this entry does not supply one.
biblical_def: Webster (1828) defines a chantry as “A church or chapel endowed with lands, or other revenue, for the maintenance of one or more priests daily to sing or say mass for the souls of the donors, or such as they appoint.” Men paid in life for prayers after death. Peter answered such a hope when Simon offered money: “Thy money perish with thee, because thou hast thought that the gift of God may be purchased with money” (Act 8:20). Redemption is “not ... with corruptible things, as silver and gold ... But with the precious blood of Christ” (1Pe 1:18–19). “None of them can by any means redeem his brother, nor give to God a ransom for him” (Psa 49:7).

pos: n. (a pointed church turret; a spire)
etymology: Webster (1828) enters STEEPLE without an etymology note; this entry does not supply one.
biblical_def: Webster (1828) defines a steeple as “A turret of a church, ending in a point; a spire.” He notes that “The bell of a church is usually hung in the steeple.” The steeple marks a place of worship from afar and calls the people with its bell. Scripture’s towers warn in two directions. Babel’s builders said, “let us build us a city and a tower, whose top may reach unto heaven; and let us make us a name” (Gen 11:4). The righteous have a better tower: “The name of the LORD is a strong tower: the righteous runneth into it, and is safe” (Pro 18:10). God “dwelleth not in temples made with hands” (Act 17:24).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): STEEPLE, a turret of a church ending in a point; a spire; the church bell usually hung in it.
webster_full: STEEPLE, noun A turret of a church, ending in a point; a spire. It differs from a tower, which usually ends in a square form, thought the name is sometimes given to a tower. The bell of a church is usually hung in the steeple

corruption_paragraphs: Webster’s steeple is one part of a building. Common speech can let the steeple stand for the church, as if the building were the body.
God does not dwell in temples made with hands (Act 17:24). Babel’s tower shows the danger of building to make a name (Gen 11:4).

etymology: Webster (1828): [Low Latin proecentor; Latin proe, before, and canto, to sing.]
biblical_def: Webster (1828) defines a precentor as “The leader of the choir in a cathedral; called also the chanter or master of the choir.” The root means one who sings before. Scripture names such leaders: “Chenaniah, chief of the Levites, was for song: he instructed about the song, because he was skilful” (1Ch 15:22). Many psalms are addressed “To the chief Musician” (Psa 4:1). In Scottish and Puritan churches the precentor lined out the psalm for the congregation to sing. The goal of any leader of song is the people’s praise: “Let the people praise thee, O God; let all the people praise thee” (Psa 67:3).

pos: n. (a singer in a choir; one who leads a choir)
etymology: Webster (1828) enters CHORISTER without an etymology note; this entry does not supply one.
biblical_def: Webster (1828) defines a chorister as “Literally, a singer; one of a choir; a singer in a concert,” and as “One who leads a choir in church music,” adding, “This is the sense in the United States.” Israel’s singers were set apart for the work: “these are the singers, chief of the fathers of the Levites ... for they were employed in that work day and night” (1Ch 9:33). At the dedication of the temple “the trumpeters and singers were as one, to make one sound to be heard in praising and thanking the LORD” (2Ch 5:13). Song is the whole church’s duty: “singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord” (Eph 5:19).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): CHORISTER, literally a singer, one of a choir; in the United States, one who leads a choir in church music.
webster_full: CHORISTER, noun
1. Literally, a singer; one of a choir; a singer in a concert.
2. One who leads a choir in church music. This is the sense in the United States.

corruption_paragraphs: Webster notes that in America the chorister was the song leader. Today the word suggests a robed boy in an English cathedral.
The temple singers sang as one to praise the LORD (2Ch 5:13). New Testament song belongs to every believer (Eph 5:19).
